abstract: This MIT FutureTech paper by Autor and colleagues presents preliminary findings from a large-scale evaluation of AI and automation's actual impact on US workers, proposing a framework that distinguishes between 'crashing waves' (sudden capability surges in specific tasks) and 'rising tides' (continuous, broad-based capability improvements). Analyzing over 3,000 text-based labor tasks from the U.S. Department of Labor O*NET database through more than 17,000 worker assessments, the researchers find minimal evidence of crashing waves but substantial evidence for rising tides as the dominant automation pattern. As of Q2 2024, AI models successfully complete tasks that take humans approximately 3-4 hours with about 50% success rate; by Q3 2025, success rates increased to approximately 65%. If current trends persist, LLMs are projected to achieve 80-95% success at minimally sufficient quality by 2029, with additional years needed for near-perfect or superior-quality performance.
keyFindings: Minimal evidence of 'crashing waves' (sudden AI capability surges) but substantial evidence for 'rising tides' (gradual, broad-based improvement) as the dominant automation pattern across 3,000+ labor tasks.
As of Q2 2024, AI models complete tasks requiring 3-4 human hours with approximately 50% success rate; by Q3 2025, success rates reached approximately 65%.
Projected trajectory: LLMs could achieve 80-95% success at minimally sufficient quality by 2029, but near-perfect or superior quality requires additional years beyond that.
The rising-tides pattern suggests workers face gradual task erosion rather than sudden displacement, allowing more time for adaptation but making the threat harder to perceive and respond to.
Over 17,000 worker evaluations provide ground-truth assessment of AI task performance, moving beyond expert judgment or model self-evaluation.
methodology: Large-scale empirical evaluation of AI capabilities across 3,000+ text-based tasks from the O*NET database, assessed through 17,000+ worker evaluations. Workers evaluated whether AI models could successfully complete specific occupational tasks at various quality thresholds. The study tracks performance trajectories from Q2 2024 through Q3 2025 and projects forward to 2029 based on observed improvement rates.
qualifiers: Explicitly labeled as preliminary findings from an ongoing evaluation — conclusions are provisional and subject to revision. Focuses on text-based tasks, potentially underestimating AI's impact on tasks involving code, data analysis, or multimodal capabilities. Success rate thresholds (minimally sufficient vs. superior quality) involve subjective worker judgments. Projections to 2029 assume continuation of current improvement trends, which may not hold if AI progress accelerates or plateaus. Does not directly measure employment or wage effects — task completion capability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for labor displacement.
